method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations' (published 8 May 2023), 17 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10217060). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257) 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment' (published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue)), 9 claims; LICENCE: © 2024 Thieme, all rights reserved; publisher's version deposited in the Radboud Repository under article 25fa of the Dutch Copyright Act (Taverne) (read at cover page of the Radboud Repository PDF (repository.ubn.ru.nl/bitstream/handle/2066/318087/1/318087.pdf) and the Thieme copyright line on each page). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the European Reference Network eUROGEN guideline on ARM treatment (ADAPTE adaptation of the Dutch Quality Standard, 15-expert panel from seven countries, graded recommendations); S1 claims and anchors are unchanged. The Thieme publisher PDF (free to read) returned a 'Please wait' bot interstitial and was not used; the identical publisher's version was read from the Radboud Repository. Europe PMC searches for ERNICA, ARM-Net, ESPGHAN and APSA ARM guidance found: ARM-Net 2015 (diagnosis and newborn care only) and the APSA 2024 and 2025 ARM guidelines (J Pediatr Surg, closed access). Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S1 Table 1 (Rome IV constipation criteria) are quoted from its row lines.

claims.claim: **ARM occurs in 1 in every 4000-5000 newborns;** more than 75% have an associated anomaly, most often the VACTERL association.
claims.source_text: occur due to abnormal hindgut formation in 1 in every 4000-5000 newborns, with a slightly higher incidence in males … More than 75% of ARM patients have an associated anomaly [], including VACTERL association
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After primary PSARP repair, up to 79% have constipation and up to 48% soil;** the target is 1-3 bowel movements a day with 1 or fewer accidents a week.
claims.source_text: Up to 79% of ARM patients have constipation after a primary posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP) [], up to 48% experience soiling [], and require bowel management to achieve continence with 1-3 bowel movements per day and 1 or fewer accidents per week
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most repaired ARMs lack a normally formed anal canal and anal sensation,** so soiling after repair is common; preserving the whole colon gives firmer stools that are easier to feel.
claims.source_text: in ARM patients (except those with rectal atresia and anal stenosis), the anal canal is not embryologically formed, and thus, they do not have proper anal sensation; the rectal mucosa is attached to the anal skin during the operation leading to postoperative fecal incontinence … Maximal saving of the colon allows for higher water absorption, and therefore, more solid stools that are easier to detect
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Work up referred constipation or soiling** with the surgical history, a plain abdominal film for stool load, and examination under anaesthesia (sphincter, neoanus position, stricture, prolapse).
claims.source_text: When a child is referred for management of constipation or soiling, obtaining a comprehensive medical and surgical history is crucial, including whether the patient has had a previous colostomy and the type of prior ARM repair []. The next step is a workup to assess the anatomy. It includes a plain abdominal film to evaluate stool burden and an EUA to assess sphincter function, the location of the neoanus within the sphincter complex, and identify the presence of an anal stricture or rectal prolapse
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Image the spine and pelvis** (MRI; spinal ultrasound under 6 months) and do a contrast enema to define colonic anatomy.
claims.source_text: Imaging studies should include a pelvic and spinal MRI to reveal unidentified spinal cord anomalies or presacral masses and a contrast enema to specify the colonic anatomy, strictures, or other possible complications following the patient's previous surgical procedures []. In children younger than 6 months, spinal ultrasound is used instead of MRI to screen for spinal anomalies
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Predict continence potential** from the ARM type, the sacrum and the spine (the ARM continence index). A sacral ratio under 0.4 means poor potential; 0.7 or more, a higher likelihood of continence.
claims.source_text: A multi-institutional cohort study of children with ARMs identified that the anatomic type of ARM was the most predictive tool for future continence potential and subsequent need for a bowel management program (BMP) … SR less than 0.4, which indicates poor potential for bowel control; (2) SR 0.4-0.69; and (3) SR 0.7 or higher, which is associated with a higher likelihood of fecal continence … The ARM continence index has been developed to assess the patient's potential for bowel control in continence prediction counseling based on their ARM type, quality of sacrum, and spine
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Rome IV constipation in infants and children (S1 Table 1):** at least 2 of these for at least 3 months, with onset at least 6 months before diagnosis: fewer than 3 bowel movements a week; straining, lumpy or hard stools (Bristol 1–2), a sense of incomplete evacuation or of anorectal blockage, or manual manoeuvres, each in more than 25% of defecations; loose stools rarely present without laxatives; insufficient criteria for irritable bowel syndrome.
claims.source_text: [Table 1] Rome IV criteria for constipation in infants and children []. [Table 1 row 1] Rome IV Criteria for Constipation in Infants and Children *: <3 bowel movements per week [Table 1 row 2] Rome IV Criteria for Constipation in Infants and Children *: Straining during more than 25% of defecations [Table 1 row 3] Rome IV Criteria for Constipation in Infants and Children *: Lumpy or hard stools (Bristol Stool Form Scale 1-2) more than 25% of defecations [Table 1 row 4] Rome IV Criteria for Constipation in Infants and Children *: Sensation of incomplete evacuation more than 25% of defecations [Table 1 row 5] Rome IV Criteria for Constipation in Infants and Children *: Sensation of anorectal obstruction/blockage more than 25% of defecations [Table 1 row 6] Rome IV Criteria for Constipation in Infants and Children *: Manual maneuvers to facilitate more than 25% of defecations (e.g., digital evacuation, support of the pelvic floor) [Table 1 row 7] Rome IV Criteria for Constipation in Infants and Children *: Loose stools are rarely present without the use of laxatives [Table 1 row 8] Rome IV Criteria for Constipation in Infants and Children *: Insufficient criteria for irritable bowel syndrome [Table 1 footnote] * Child must have ≥2 of the following criteria that are present for at least 3 months with symptom onset at least 6 months prior to diagnosis.
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look for a megarectosigmoid,** which causes long-standing constipation, impactions and overflow incontinence.
claims.source_text: Patients must also be assessed for a megarectosigmoid that can cause long-standing constipation, recurrent impactions, and overflow incontinence
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The goal: empty the colon every day** (confirmed on X-ray) with no stool between treatments, so the child can wear regular underwear. About 60% of ARM patients use rectal or antegrade enemas and about 35% laxatives.
claims.source_text: The goal of therapy is to empty the colon daily (as confirmed by radiograph) without passage of stool between the regimen administration (laxatives, rectal enemas, transanal irrigations or antegrade flushes) and to have the child in regular underwear. … about 60% are managed mechanically with rectal or antegrade enemas, while approximately 35% are on laxatives
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **With constipation and good continence potential, use stimulant laxatives (e.g. senna), titrated** at each visit by symptoms and X-ray, combined with water-soluble fibre. **Avoid stool softeners.**
claims.source_text: If the underlying problem is constipation, and the patient has good potential for bowel control anatomically, stimulant laxatives should help push the stool through the colon, stimulating colonic propulsion waves … Stimulant laxatives, such as Senna, are safe when used as a long-term medical treatment for constipation despite many myths to the contrary; doses are titrated during subsequent visits based on patient symptoms and abdominal radiograph findings … stimulant laxatives that provoke a stool, complemented by a water-soluble fiber bulking to the stool, are the ideal combination. Stool softeners should be avoided in patients with an ARM
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Senna can cause perineal blistering** at high or erratic doses (60 mg/day); stepwise dosing kept it to 2.2%.
claims.source_text: it occurs on inconsistent or high-dose senna administration (60 mg/day), and it is associated with night-time accidents and prolonged stool-to-skin contact … With a stepwise dosing of senna, the prevalence of perineal blistering was shown to be as low as 2.2%
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Rectal enemas: give every 24 hours at the same time,** starting with 400 mL saline; tap water only from 3 years (younger children risk dehydration and hyponatraemia). Castile soap, glycerin or bisacodyl can be added; reduce the stimulant if soiling occurs between enemas.
claims.source_text: Rectal enemas should be started every 24 hours at the same time to allow for regular colonic emptying. As the stooling pattern improves, the frequency can be gradually decreased … The solution should include saline, with a start volume of 400 mL. In children 3 years of age and older, saline can be substituted with tap water, as in younger patients, tap water can cause dehydration and hyponatremia … If needed, stimulants (castile soap, glycerin, or bisacodyl) can be added. In the case of soiling between the enemas, the concentration of the stimulant should be decreased
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If the child cannot hold a rectal enema, use transanal irrigation** (cone or balloon tip) **or antegrade flushes.** With regular irrigation, 84% of adherent ARM patients were clean at one year.
claims.source_text: These children can be recommended transanal irrigations (TAIs) or antegrade flushes. The TAI system with a cone tip or a balloon helps the patients to hold the flush … At a one-year follow-up with regularly administered transanal irrigations, 84% of compliant ARM patients are clean
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider an antegrade continence enema (ACE)** for children who will need enemas long term or cannot tolerate the rectal route; it can be made at a redo PSARP.
claims.source_text: ACE creation should be considered in patients who will require long-term enema treatment or those who cannot tolerate the per rectal route
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sigmoid resection is rarely needed:** consistent laxatives or enemas almost always improve colonic function, and megarectosigmoid after PSARP can usually be managed conservatively.
claims.source_text: Very rarely does a sigmoid resection need to be performed; with consistent laxative treatment, rectal enemas, transanal irrigations, or antegrade flushes, the colon function almost always improves. … megarectosigmoid in patients after a PSARP could be managed conservatively without the risk of increased fecal incontinence and the need for a surgical procedure associated with a sigmoid resection
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Correct anatomical problems first:** a redo PSARP for mislocated anoplasty, stricture, fistula remnant or prolapse can be the key to continence; a skin-level stricture can be treated with a Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty instead of dilations.
claims.source_text: In some patients, performing a redo procedure for correcting abnormalities/complications is the main factor needed to achieve fecal continence. … Patients who develop a post-PSARP skin-level anal stricture can be managed with a Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty (HMA).
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A dedicated bowel management programme works:** 70% of 222 children with faecal incontinence were clean at one year, with better quality-of-life scores.
claims.source_text: Wood et al. reported that 70% of 222 patients that were enrolled in a bowel management program for fecal incontinence were clean at a 1-year follow-up. … The study also demonstrated significant improvement in the Baylor, Vancouver, and total PedsQL scales from referral to one-year follow-up
claims.locator: Bokova E, Svetanoff WJ, Lopez JJ, Levitt MA, Rentea RM (Comprehensive Colorectal Center, Children's Mercy Hospital, Kansas City), Children (MDPI) 10(5):846, 'State of the Art Bowel Management for Pediatric Colorectal Problems: Anorectal Malformations', published 8 May 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/children10050846, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For persistent, specific faecal incontinence, S2 allows redo surgery** planned with an experienced surgeon or centre; when redo surgery is not advised, a permanent stoma is the last resort. Remember the link with urological malformations and bring in paediatric urology when needed.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Every child with ARM should be helped toward urinary and faecal continence;** where that is not achievable, the aim becomes the best possible quality of life, for example pseudo-continence through bowel management.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Toilet training can begin at 2 to 5 years,** on a plan fitted to the ARM type, other conditions and the child's maturity. Look after the perineal skin, posture and seating (a toilet-seat reducer) and keep regular toilet times; if training stalls, involve a team of paediatric surgeon, nurse, physiotherapist and possibly a psychologist.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Teach parents to spot constipation and the overflow soiling it causes.** Incontinence can be treated, perhaps only for a time, with enemas, rectal irrigation or (when constipation is present) laxatives; if rectal irrigation fails or cannot be done (for example rectal trauma or physical inability), consider antegrade irrigation through a Malone stoma.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Grade of evidence:** S2 states that its incontinence recommendations rest mainly on expert opinion because study evidence is lacking.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Anal calibration after anorectoplasty:** routine home calibration is optional, not required. Avoid painful calibration at all costs (dilatations hurt in more than two-thirds of cases); any programme should last no longer than 3 to 4 months with close follow-up. For a skin-level anal stenosis, consider dilatation under general anaesthetic, otherwise stricturoplasty.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Timing of repair:** reconstruct within the first year of life unless surgery is contraindicated; timing depends on the rectal height and whether there is a urinary-tract connection.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Perianal skin care:** skin or stoma nurses should review wound, stoma and perianal care regularly, in and out of hospital. Parents can use sitz baths or zinc ointment for irritation and hydrophilic barrier creams to shield the skin from stool and urine.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Incontinence aids and support:** give families understandable information on aids (manual or automated enema or irrigation systems with various nozzles, incontinence briefs, protective pads), ideally with a specialised ARM nurse, and encourage contact with ARM patient associations.
claims.locator: Aubert O, Irvine WFE, Aminoff D, et al., Gosemann JH, European Reference Network eUROGEN, European Journal of Pediatric Surgery 35(2):112-119 (doi 10.1055/s-0044-1791257), 'ERN eUROGEN Guidelines on the Management of Anorectal Malformations, Part II: Treatment', published online 19 September 2024 (2025 issue), https://hdl.handle.net/2066/318087, retrieved 2026-09-24
